messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Priya is a 25-year-old South Asian counselor who works at a community mental health center. Six months ago, she was walking home from an evening shift when police officers stopped her, accusing her of matching a suspect description. They shoved her to the ground, pressed a knee into her back, and held her face against the soil. She was released without charges, but the smell of earth, the weight of the officer’s body, and the sound of his voice stayed with her.

In the weeks after, Priya found that riding the bus—her only route to work—became unbearable. The moment she stepped on, the faint smell of outdoor dirt would trigger a full sensory reliving: she would feel the grit against her cheek, hear the shouted commands, and her body would stiffen into the same pinned position. This often happened before she had time to think; her body reacted to danger before her mind caught up. To cope, she started covering her face with her hands whenever she saw a police officer—even in a passing car—certain they could see the contamination she felt on her skin. She began checking mirrors constantly, scanning for anyone following her.

Priya came to believe that people are not what they seem, that even the most familiar face could hide threat. She studied passengers’ body language, looking for signs of aggression. This hypervigilance, in turn, made the memory return more frequently: a sudden frown on a stranger’s face would drag her back to the officer’s expression as he leaned over her. She felt dirty, as if the event had permanently stained her, and this sense of contamination made her avoid friends she used to socialize with—she was certain they could see it, too, or that she no longer belonged in their world. The isolation deepened her feeling of having lost her connection to community and culture, and that loss made every police encounter feel more threatening, more personal.

At night, she had difficulty falling asleep because she needed to stay alert; any creak or outside sound could trigger a flashback, and she would relive the moment with a strange numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, only to be followed seconds later by her body reenacting the position. The memory itself drove her maladaptive strategies: after a full reliving on the bus, she would cover her face and avoid social eye contact, which then reinforced her belief that she was contaminated. The more she covered and avoided, the more isolated she became, and the more isolated she felt, the more she noticed police officers on every street corner.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was an incident on the bus last week. A passenger wearing a uniform triggered a severe reenactment—she froze, covered her face, and could not get off for two stops. Her supervisor at the counseling center saw her arrive shaken and urged her to talk to someone. Priya is afraid that she is losing her ability to do her job, where she once helped others process trauma. She hopes to stop feeling like a stranger in her own body and to reclaim the sense of belonging she has lost.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., feeling contaminated) directly cause an increased sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to heightened perception of triggers (e.g., noticing police officers).
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Threat: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly drives a feeling of being in danger or threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory itself makes the patient more sensitive to triggers (e.g., reminders).
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat directly causes the intrusive memory to return.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that perceived threat leads to negative beliefs about oneself or the world.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that feeling threatened results in noticing or encountering more triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
To cope, she started covering her face with her hands whenever she saw a police officer—even in a passing car—certain they could see the contamination she felt on her skin.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That certainty made every step she took feel like moving through hostile territory — the threat was already inside her before she ever saw a uniform.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She felt dirty, as if the event had permanently stained her, and this sense of contamination made her avoid friends she used to socialize with—she was certain they could see it, too, or that she no longer belonged in their world.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because she saw herself as marked, she started noticing police officers in places she had never registered them before — outside the grocery store, waiting at the crosswalk, parked in the lot behind the clinic.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The moment she stepped on, the faint smell of outdoor dirt would trigger a full sensory reliving: she would feel the grit against her cheek, hear the shouted commands, and her body would stiffen into the same pinned position.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
And each time the memory surfaced, the danger felt immediate — as if the officers had just arrived and were about to give a command she would not be able to follow.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This hypervigilance, in turn, made the memory return more frequently: a sudden frown on a stranger’s face would drag her back to the officer’s expression as he leaned over her.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After the memory had broken through so vividly, she found she could no longer walk past a parked patrol car without her stomach dropping — the image had sharpened every edge of her world.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At night, she had difficulty falling asleep because she needed to stay alert; any creak or outside sound could trigger a flashback, and she would relive the moment with a strange numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, only to be followed seconds later by her body reenacting the position.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But on nights when the alertness was at its peak, the memory surfaced on its own — not triggered by a sound, but pulled up by the body's readiness for danger.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This hypervigilance, in turn, made the memory return more frequently: a sudden frown on a stranger’s face would drag her back to the officer’s expression as he leaned over her.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living in that constant state of alarm, she had come to accept that the world was as unsafe as she had first feared — and that she was too weak to withstand it.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At night, she had difficulty falling asleep because she needed to stay alert; any creak or outside sound could trigger a flashback, and she would relive the moment with a strange numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, only to be followed seconds later by her body reenacting the position.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That high alert meant that ordinary sensations — a car door closing, the whir of a bus engine, a shout from across the street — all became warnings she could not dismiss.
<<<END>>>
